There is real fear that Nvidia might pull back on their investments and backstops. 
 
I believe this is misplaced. Nvidia’s competitors are eager to take their place, disrupt their relationships and fill any vacuum left by Nvidia.
 
There are at least three companies aggressively vying to be the new “Central Bank” of AI.
 
Across many @atreidesmgmt venture portfolio companies we are seeing Nvidia’s semiconductor and hyperscale competitors trying to lean in and displace Nvidia in important relationships. Ironically, sometimes at more favorable terms than those offered by Nvidia.
 
And of course, also beginning to see the first signs of Nvidia waking up to this risk and addressing it. Their strategic imperatives have not changed and their strategy was sound, but there is only one Jensen and competitors are now attempting to really take advantage of his absence. No one wants a monopsony at the lab layer.
 
I suspect the same thing is happening in the supply chain. But again, there is only one Jensen.

$P earnings were actually interesting, not really in terms actionable investments. 

But more on AI capex broadening, where deployments are happening, and what Jensen at $NVDA might envisioned with open weight model + GPU demand. 

- Everpure CEO stated that enterprises are increasingly building on-premises AI factories, stating: 

"The ROI for companies to buy their own GPU environments and run their own models is starting to come to the forefront."

- "I'm talking about standard enterprises, regular finance organizations. A wide variety of organizations are starting to buy these AI factories for the purpose of running their own open weight models

From "regular insurance companies, et cetera"

- "One is they're starting to see that these open weight models are actually being able to provide good results, and they're doing so at a fraction of the cost of using the cloud for these workloads"

"that the ROI for companies to buy their own GPU environments and run their own models is starting to come to the forefront"

This type of broad industry transition would be heavily bearish as it threatens $ANT, OpenAI and frontier labs over the long term... 

And probably what Jensen saw things heading with $NVDA + additional GPU demand regardless of what frontier lab wins. 

However, I expect more of the open weight effort to collapse or see heavier regulation with how Washington + frontier labs were lobbying. 

- In regards to NAND prices dropping: "If prices come down slowly, I expect to see demand come up along with that" (Jevon) 

- LOL this part was hilarious and the same argument I was using for why qualification cycle players like in optics were so interesting. 

On data center slowdown potential:

"So on the first part of it, remember, I mean, really, the thing that insulates us is we have such a small share going into the hyperscale market"

"even in a down market, they’re going to spend a lot more than our current share amounts to", and their market capture goes up over time relative to overall TAM.

Crypto feels dead right now.

But in 2021, blockchains took 62% of crypto fees. Today, apps take over 95%.

Need some hopium?

Here are 4 areas of crypto still making real progress:

1. Tokens that buy themselves back

For years, the whole plan for most tokens was "buy it and hope someone else pays more later." Not exactly a business model.

Now Hyperliquid, Uniswap and pump .fun use their revenue to buy back or burn their own tokens. Hyperliquid especially, since it makes serious money from real trading.

That means usage can create demand for the token even when nobody's in the mood to buy. Basically, the protocol is the one buyer that never panic sells.

Unlocks still matter, so check that the buybacks are bigger than the new supply hitting the market.

2. Private AI is becoming a real business

Privacy has become one of the more interesting sectors this cycle, and Zcash is getting a lot of renewed interest.

The one I'm watching most closely is Venice. It sells private AI access and uses part of what people pay to buy back and burn $VVV.

New tokens are still being created faster than they're burned, though, so I'm watching it rather than buying it yet.

3. Wall Street is still moving onchain

About $39B of real-world assets, not counting stablecoins, are already tokenized.

Even with everyone scared, BlackRock and other big firms keep bringing traditional financial products onto blockchain rails. They're not checking the Fear & Greed Index every morning like the rest of us. They're planning for years, not weeks.

4. Stablecoins don't need a bull market

There's about $284B in stablecoins today, and more companies are using them to send money across borders.

Tether, Circle and Stripe are all building around this.

A business paying someone overseas doesn't care what BTC did this week. It just wants the money to arrive faster and cheaper, without a bank calling it "3 to 5 business days."

What I'm doing with this

The Fear & Greed Index is at 12, while these businesses keep building.

I'm lining up projects from these four areas and looking for ones where revenue is growing while the price keeps falling. That's the setup I want to be early on when sentiment flips.

I don't know if that's next month or next year, and plenty of tokens won't make it back. But the businesses are still running.

What part of crypto gives you the most conviction right now?

“Ben Graham, my friend and teacher, long ago described the mental attitude toward market fluctuations that I believe to be most conducive to investment success. He said that you should imagine market quotations as coming from a remarkably accommodating fellow named Mr. Market who is your partner in a private business. Without fail, Mr. Market appears daily and names a price at which he will either buy your interest or sell you his. 

Even though the business that the two of you own may have economic characteristics that are stable, Mr. Market's quotations will be anything but. For, sad to say, the poor fellow has incurable emotional problems. At times he feels euphoric and can see only the favorable factors affecting the business. When in that mood, he names a very high buy-sell price because he fears that you will snap up his interest and rob him of imminent gains. At other times he is depressed and can see nothing but trouble ahead for both the business and the world. On these occasions he will name a very low price, since he is terrified that you will unload your interest on him.

Mr. Market has another endearing characteristic: He doesn't mind being ignored. If his quotation is uninteresting to you today, he will be back with a new one tomorrow. Transactions are strictly at your option.

Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you."

- Warren Buffet (1987 Shareholder Letter)

In spring the market was also very worried about AI killing cybersecurity and infrastructure software companies and that turned out to be dead wrong. 

The jury is still out on how the Dems sweep will impact the AI capex cycle and how Nvidia's next CEO will manage the business. During times like these when most are super bearish and sentiment is super negative, best to remain calm and focus on the facts.

tweets.text: This conference season, Ayar Labs put real manufacturing statistics on its SuperNova ELSFPs. More than 100 laser units were measured at 50 C with -20 dB back reflections to simulate imperfections in fiber connectors and fiber-to-PIC coupling. The notable stats include a mean RIN of -158 dB/Hz and an especially low mean linewidth of 0.16 MHz, comparable to what 400ZR coherent class lasers are specified at; giving a lot of margin for DWDM operation. Importantly, every laser met spec with margin, which matters a lot more in production than one device achieving extraordinary performance.
